A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UniFL research, with matching authors, methods, and experiments. The main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–D are readable and support comparison despite substantial reformatting and renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on synthetic geometric graphs and city road networks, including solution costs, runtimes, size generalization, and clustering comparisons.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds results on degree-shift generalization and training with structurally diverse graphs.

M1.justification: The radius-based MPNN, expected-cost loss, probabilistic facility opening, recursive algorithms, and squared-distance clustering variant remain unchanged. Mixed-distribution training changes the experimental data, without introducing a new architecture, objective, or inference procedure.

E1.justification: V2 adds explicit transfer scenarios involving denser 2D geometric graphs with average degrees 10, 12, 17, 22, and 27. This extends input-distribution coverage within the existing UniFL domain; the original dimensions, city networks, clustering tasks, and size-transfer coverage remain.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparators remain the ILP solver, SimpleUniformFL, RecursiveUFL, Gehweiler et al.'s algorithm, and the same clustering alternatives. O(1)-UFL explicitly denotes the previously evaluated Gehweiler et al. algorithm; it is not a new baseline.

E3.justification: V2 adds evaluation without fine-tuning on denser graphs and a mixed-training experiment using 10,000 samples with 800–1200 nodes and average degrees 5–15. Table 8 also corrects four graph-order entries from v1 Table 4, including Geo-10000-2 from 5,000 to 10,000 nodes. These corrections do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Tables 4–6 substantially extend the generalization analysis: they test sensitivity to neighborhood density, examine mixed-distribution training as a mitigation, and check whether that training preserves size transfer. V1's transfer analysis varied graph size while keeping average degree approximately stable.

E5.justification: Both versions report five independent training runs with means and standard deviations, and 1,000 stochastic samples per instance. The added tables follow the existing uncertainty-reporting practice; no new confidence intervals, significance tests, or increased run counts are reported.

E6.justification: Tables 4–6 add substantial generalization results. Table 4 reports the original 2D model's ratio rising from 1.009 on its original distribution to 1.124 at degree 17; Table 6 reports 1.008 on that same degree-17 test set for the mixed-trained model. These are results under different training conditions. All numerical entries in the matched pre-existing result tables remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical statements and proof arguments are retained. V1 Proposition 5 and its appendix proof remain as v2 Lemma 13 despite removal of the duplicate main-text statement. V1 Proposition 6 becomes v2 Proposition 5, retaining the same fixed-size generalization statement and proof in Appendix C.4.

C1.justification: The abstract drops the claim of provable size generalization, and introduction contribution 3 changes from generalizing to arbitrarily large instances to instances of the same size. This substantially narrows a central claimed contribution. The revision is incomplete: the conclusion still claims provable transfer to arbitrarily larger graphs.

C2.justification: Section 4.1 adds a focused explanation that size transfer preserves familiar local neighborhoods when degree stays stable, whereas density changes shift aggregated messages. It identifies structural diversity in training as a mitigation. The broader limitations concerning richer facility-location variants and optimization guarantees remain unchanged.

D1.justification: V2 documents the new mixed dataset's sample count, node-count range, and degree range, and corrects dataset-size information in Appendix D. Existing model depths, hidden dimensions, training limits, baseline tuning, hardware, and implementation descriptions remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds Beaini et al. (2023) and Zhao et al. (2024) to motivate diverse pretraining, and connects the new density findings to the already cited Levin et al. (2025). The main related-work positioning remains stable; Wittig's publication update refers to the same previously cited work.

P1.justification: The abstract is condensed and rewritten, terminology and sentences receive local edits, Section 3.4's heading is shortened, and an impact statement is added. The duplicate recursive-cost proposition is removed from the main text while retained in the appendix. The overall section sequence remains intact.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from a single-column manuscript to a two-column conference layout, with extensive resizing and repositioning of displays. V2 adds Tables 4–6 and moves the unchanged city-map results from v1 appendix Table 6 to main-text Table 2. Both original figures remain.

improvement.justification: V2 improves the empirical account of generalization by exposing density-related degradation and testing mixed training on matching test sets. It also corrects dataset sizes and narrows the introductory claim to match the unchanged fixed-size theorem. These gains are limited by the unreconciled arbitrary-size guarantee in the conclusion and a new reporting error: the density discussion quotes 1.002 where Table 4 reports 1.009.
